Times Higher Education World University Rankings
Times Higher Education (THE) publishes its World University Rankings, often shortened to THE WUR, every September or October. This flagship table compares research-intensive universities worldwide across five pillars: teaching, research environment, research quality, industry and international outlook. The current method, WUR 3.0, was first used in the 2024 edition, and the 2027 edition scores 17 indicators. Citation measures make up about 30% of the total and THE's teaching and research reputation surveys another third, so the table says more about a university's research strength and academic standing than about the quality of its teaching. Here you will find every ranked university with the overall and pillar scores THE published; search by name, filter by country or territory, or switch to an earlier edition. Editions up to 2023 used the previous method, so read any move across the 2024 change with care.
Edition commentary THE World University Rankings 2027: Tsinghua rises to 11th, ahead of ETH Zurich Hayden Young · 2026-09-30
Times Higher Education World University Rankings methodology: indicators, weights and data sources  
THE assesses institutions across five pillars: Teaching, Research Environment, Research Quality, Industry and International Outlook.

## How do the Times Higher Education World University Rankings evaluate universities?
The rankings group their indicators into five pillars, scored from THE's annual Academic Reputation Survey, publications and citations in Elsevier's Scopus database, and figures the universities submit; the weighted pillars add up to an overall score, and lower positions are published as bands. They are compiled by Times Higher Education (THE), a London-based higher-education magazine and data company, and the table shows the overall and pillar scores it published. To be ranked, a university has to teach undergraduates and clear a publication threshold (more than 1,000 papers over five years in the 2027 edition). The 2027 edition ranks 2,297 institutions from 117 countries and regions. Another 849 are listed without a rank. In recent editions THE lists universities that submitted data but missed the threshold as "Reporter", by name only, with no rank or score. THE changed its method in the 2024 edition (WUR 3.0), so check the methodology page before comparing ranks across years. XuanXiao records the ranks and scores THE published, and this page links to THE's own table.

## Which are the top universities in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2027?
The leading places in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2027 are held by University of Oxford (1), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (2), Princeton University (=3), Stanford University (=3), University of Cambridge (5), Harvard University (6), California Institute of Technology (7), Imperial College London (8), University of California, Berkeley (=9), Yale University (=9); a rank marked "=" is shared. The 2027 edition ranks 2,297 institutions from 117 countries and regions. Another 849 are listed without a rank. This ranking is published by Times Higher Education, and the table below gives every institution its position and the scores Times Higher Education released. Methodologies differ widely between rankings, so read them alongside your own subject, region and career goals.

## How do the Times Higher Education World University Rankings differ from other ranking systems?
THE spreads its weight more evenly than the other three. In the 2027 edition its 17 indicators sit in five pillars: teaching (29.5%), research environment (29%), research quality (30%), industry (4%) and international outlook (7.5%). Grouped the way the comparison table groups them, reputation surveys count for 33% (teaching and research reputation together) and citation measures for 30%; the rest goes to teaching resources, research income and output, industry and international outlook. Its data come from THE's Academic Reputation Survey, Elsevier's Scopus and figures the universities submit. By comparison, QS puts 45% on its academic and employer surveys, ARWU uses no survey and counts Nobel Prizes, Fields Medals, highly cited researchers and papers, and U.S. News gives half its weight to citation measures. THE suits readers who want one table that weighs reputation, research and teaching resources together.

About Leiden University
Basic information and contact details for Leiden University
Founded in 1575, Leiden University is the first university in the Netherlands and a broad, internationally oriented research university. Across seven faculties in two cities, Leiden and The Hague, more than 33,000 students from 120 nationalities learn to tackle the challenges of today and tomorrow.

Are you curious, critical and involved in the world around you? At Leiden University you can make a valuable contribution to tackling the national and international challenges facing modern society. Together with academics and fellow students from all over the world, you will actively address these challenges. We keep an open mind, do not shy away from difficult discussions and allow one another the space to disagree. We expect the same active, open-minded and critical attitude from you.
Bastion of freedom. William of Orange founded the university in 1575, it is said in recognition of the city's courageous resistance against the Spanish siege. Our motto, Praesidium Libertatis (bastion of freedom), still guides us: we place great value on freedom of thought, inquiry and speech. Sixteen Nobel Prize winners have been connected to Leiden.
Teaching with personal attention. Our teaching is characterised by individual attention for students, contact with diverse cultures and innovative teaching methods. Our modest community size in the historical cities of Leiden and The Hague creates a personal and committed atmosphere. Together, we map out a learning path that suits you and your ambitions, and you are encouraged to conduct research with eminent and enthusiastic scholars. Teaching and research are closely interwoven.
Research that matters. Our research and teaching inspire one another, and this cross-pollination shapes our contribution to society. We train our students to become analytical thinkers and critical world citizens who can apply their knowledge to make the world a safe, healthy, sustainable, prosperous and just place.
Two cities, one university. Leiden is a real student city: a historic and lively centre with university buildings, student associations, cafés and housing within cycling distance. The Hague, the city of peace and justice, is the political heart of the Netherlands and home to embassies, multinationals and international courts. Teaching and research at Campus The Hague focus on international law, peace and security, global affairs, governance and urban issues. The cities themselves are the campus.

Programmes. Leiden offers 51 bachelor's programmes and 83 master's programmes, many of them taught in English, across Archaeology, Governance and Global Affairs, Humanities, Law, Medicine, Science, and Social and Behavioural Sciences. Explore our master's programmes, or read about admission and application. (https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/education/masters?utm_source=THE&utm_medium=portal&utm_campaign=Enhanced+Profile&utm_content=description_masters), (https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/education/admission-and-application?utm_source=THE&utm_medium=portal&utm_campaign=Enhanced+Profile&utm_content=description_admission).
Support and career. Every faculty has its own career services, open to students and to alumni for up to one year after graduation. Career counsellors help with internships, job applications and planning your next step, in the Netherlands or abroad. Leiden's lecturers and professors bring an extensive network of international organisations, companies and research institutes.
More than our rank. Leiden University often appears high in international rankings, but we encourage you to look beyond them and explore who we are: a university that values academic freedom, open debate and an engaged community. Find out why students choose Leiden (https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/education/masters/why-leiden-university?utm_source=THE&utm_medium=portal&utm_campaign=Enhanced+Profile&utm_content=description_why_leiden).
Leiden University welcomes anyone who wants to achieve their full potential. The knowledge and skills you develop here will benefit you for the rest of your life, whatever career path you choose.

Six universities in the Netherlands have ranked in the top 100 universities worldwide, according to the World University Rankings 2024, as compiled by Times Higher Education. Delft retains its spot as the best university overall in the Netherlands.

# 6 Dutch universities ranked among the top 100 in the world
## World University Rankings 2024 studies institutions in 166 different countries
The Times Higher Education ranking scores universities on 18 carefully selected performance indicators, updated this year to reflect the outputs of the diverse range of universities located across the world.
These performance indicators are grouped into five areas: Teaching (the learning environment); Research environment (volume, income and reputation); Research quality (citation impact, research strength, research excellence and research influence); International outlook (staff, students and research); and Industry (income and patents).
Naturally, not all of these areas have an equal weight in the ranking, with Teaching weighted at 29,5 percent, Research Environment at 29 percent, Research Quality at 30 percent, International Outlook at 7,5 percent and Industry at 4 percent. The ranking looks at data, combined with the results of the Academic Reputation Survey 2023, where more than 500.000 votes were analysed to draw conclusions about universities in 166 different countries.

# 6 Dutch universities ranked among the top 100 in the world
## Six Dutch universities make the top 100 in the World University Rankings 2024
The six Dutch universities featured in the top 100 are: Delft University of Technology, the University of Amsterdam, Wageningen University and Research, Leiden University, University of Groningen and the Erasmus University Rotterdam. The top Dutch university, Delft, came in 48th place, ahead of its 2023 spot in 70th position.
TU Delft is a research university home to around 16.000 students, many of whom are international students, which produces world-leading research and has strong strategic partnerships with industry, including many Dutch companies.The university offers all of its master’s degree programmes in English. However those looking to undertake an undergraduate degree at the school will first need to do a few Dutch courses, since most of them are taught in Dutch.
The Dutch university in the lowest spot, according to the ranking, is Tilburg University. Interestingly, the Dutch university with the lowest number of international students was named as Radboud University (ranked 140th), where of the 23.004 students, only 12 percent are internationals.

# 6 Dutch universities ranked among the top 100 in the world
## Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2024
The top Dutch universities for 2024 according to the World University Rankings are:
*   48. Delft University of Technology  
*   61. University of Amsterdam  
*   64. Wageningen University and Research  
*   77. Leiden University  
*   79. University of Groningen  
*   99. Erasmus University Rotterdam
As for the global top 10, the winners are:
*   1. University of Oxford  
*   2. Stanford University  
*   3. Massachusetts University of Technology  
*   4. Harvard University  
*   5. University of Cambridge  
*   6. Princeton University  
*   7. California Institute of Technology  
*   8. Imperial College London  
*   9. University of California, Berkeley  
*   10. Yale University
For the full list of universities, or more information on how the list was compiled, see the Times Higher Education website.

# Benjamin TORAMAN’s Post
## More Relevant Posts
Universities are not facing a single “future challenge”. They are navigating several forces at once, and those forces often pull in different directions. A few reflections from today’s European University Association (EUA) Masterclass (which was very well organised, by the way): 1. Political shifts can affect trust in expertise and the space universities have to contribute to public debate. 2. Economic pressure shapes what institutions can invest in and how secure academic careers feel. 3. Technological change, especially AI, is reshaping expectations around teaching, research and the skills academics need. 4. Societal change brings new demands for relevance, inclusion and flexibility. 5. Environmental challenges are prompting universities to rethink their responsibilities and long-term choices. What interests me most is how these developments connect, and how well universities can respond to change across all these areas. Expectations to contribute through teaching, research, public engagement and collaboration can expand academic workloads. Within that complexity, one question keeps resurfacing: what kinds of academic work are recognised when careers progress? One theme in today’s discussions that resonated with me was the recognition of teaching in academic careers. Teaching is central to a university’s purpose, yet its place in career progression remains an important question across higher education. The discussion also raised a broader challenge: staff development cannot simply mean adding new skills to already full workloads. It depends on whether institutions create the time, pathways and recognition that allow people to develop and contribute sustainably. No final answers yet, but at least the way forward comes with a rather impressive staircase 🙂 Lithuanian University of Health Sciences

# Benjamin TORAMAN’s Post
## More Relevant Posts
The Research Science Institute (RSI) is one of the most prestigious and selective summer research programs in the world for high school students. Each summer, only 100 students are selected to take part at MIT; the acceptance rate is around 2%, the program is completely free, and close to one third of its participants come from outside the United States. And starting in 2027, this opportunity will also expand to Stanford University. For six weeks, selected students do far more than simply take a course at MIT. They work with researchers, develop an original scientific project, write a research paper, and present their results at the RSI Symposium. It is an experience designed for students who have already taken mathematics, physics, biology, computer science, or engineering far beyond what is normally studied in high school. In the new RUTA blog article, we explain what the Research Science Institute really is, how it began, who can apply, how the application process works for U.S. and international students, what kind of profiles are typically selected, what happens during the six weeks, and why RSI can become one of the strongest academic experiences in a STEM profile. We also discuss an important distinction that many families do not fully understand: not every summer program that carries the name of a prestigious university has the same academic value. Spending a few weeks studying at Harvard, Columbia, Brown, Cornell, Georgetown, or NYU is very different from earning a place in a highly selective program such as RSI, SSP, or PROMYS, where admission itself already represents a significant academic distinction. And the next edition will be especially interesting. In 2027, RSI will keep its 100 places at MIT and add another 50 at Stanford, marking the largest expansion in the program’s history. Studying in the Netherlands is becoming more and more popular among international students, partly because of the ample array of world-leading Dutch universities that teach in English.

About Leiden University
Basic information and contact details for Leiden University
Founded in 1575, Leiden University is the first university in the Netherlands and a broad, internationally oriented research university. Across seven faculties in two cities, Leiden and The Hague, more than 33,000 students from 120 nationalities learn to tackle the challenges of today and tomorrow.
texts.1:
Are you curious, critical and involved in the world around you? At Leiden University you can make a valuable contribution to tackling the national and international challenges facing modern society. Together with academics and fellow students from all over the world, you will actively address these challenges. We keep an open mind, do not shy away from difficult discussions and allow one another the space to disagree. We expect the same active, open-minded and critical attitude from you.
Bastion of freedom. William of Orange founded the university in 1575, it is said in recognition of the city's courageous resistance against the Spanish siege. Our motto, Praesidium Libertatis (bastion of freedom), still guides us: we place great value on freedom of thought, inquiry and speech. Sixteen Nobel Prize winners have been connected to Leiden.
Teaching with personal attention. Our teaching is characterised by individual attention for students, contact with diverse cultures and innovative teaching methods. Our modest community size in the historical cities of Leiden and The Hague creates a personal and committed atmosphere. Together, we map out a learning path that suits you and your ambitions, and you are encouraged to conduct research with eminent and enthusiastic scholars. Teaching and research are closely interwoven.
Research that matters. Our research and teaching inspire one another, and this cross-pollination shapes our contribution to society. We train our students to become analytical thinkers and critical world citizens who can apply their knowledge to make the world a safe, healthy, sustainable, prosperous and just place.
Two cities, one university. Leiden is a real student city: a historic and lively centre with university buildings, student associations, cafés and housing within cycling distance. The Hague, the city of peace and justice, is the political heart of the Netherlands and home to embassies, multinationals and international courts. Teaching and research at Campus The Hague focus on international law, peace and security, global affairs, governance and urban issues. The cities themselves are the campus.
texts.2:
Programmes. Leiden offers 51 bachelor's programmes and 83 master's programmes, many of them taught in English, across Archaeology, Governance and Global Affairs, Humanities, Law, Medicine, Science, and Social and Behavioural Sciences. Support and career. Every faculty has its own career services, open to students and to alumni for up to one year after graduation. Career counsellors help with internships, job applications and planning your next step, in the Netherlands or abroad. Leiden's lecturers and professors bring an extensive network of international organisations, companies and research institutes.
More than our rank. Leiden University often appears high in international rankings, but we encourage you to look beyond them and explore who we are: a university that values academic freedom, open debate and an engaged community. Find out why students choose Leiden (https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/education/masters/why-leiden-university?utm_source=THE&utm_medium=portal&utm_campaign=Enhanced+Profile&utm_content=description_why_leiden).

texts.1:
# 6 Dutch universities ranked among the top 100 in the world
## World University Rankings 2024 studies institutions in 166 different countries
The Times Higher Education ranking scores universities on 18 carefully selected performance indicators, updated this year to reflect the outputs of the diverse range of universities located across the world.
These performance indicators are grouped into five areas: Teaching (the learning environment); Research environment (volume, income and reputation); Research quality (citation impact, research strength, research excellence and research influence); International outlook (staff, students and research); and Industry (income and patents).
Naturally, not all of these areas have an equal weight in the ranking, with Teaching weighted at 29,5 percent, Research Environment at 29 percent, Research Quality at 30 percent, International Outlook at 7,5 percent and Industry at 4 percent. The ranking looks at data, combined with the results of the Academic Reputation Survey 2023, where more than 500.000 votes were analysed to draw conclusions about universities in 166 different countries.
texts.2:
# 6 Dutch universities ranked among the top 100 in the world
## Six Dutch universities make the top 100 in the World University Rankings 2024
The six Dutch universities featured in the top 100 are: Delft University of Technology, the University of Amsterdam, Wageningen University and Research, Leiden University, University of Groningen and the Erasmus University Rotterdam. The top Dutch university, Delft, came in 48th place, ahead of its 2023 spot in 70th position.
TU Delft is a research university home to around 16.000 students, many of whom are international students, which produces world-leading research and has strong strategic partnerships with industry, including many Dutch companies.The university offers all of its master’s degree programmes in English. However those looking to undertake an undergraduate degree at the school will first need to do a few Dutch courses, since most of them are taught in Dutch.
The Dutch university in the lowest spot, according to the ranking, is Tilburg University. Interestingly, the Dutch university with the lowest number of international students was named as Radboud University (ranked 140th), where of the 23.004 students, only 12 percent are internationals.

Universities are not facing a single “future challenge”. They are navigating several forces at once, and those forces often pull in different directions. A few reflections from today’s European University Association (EUA) Masterclass (which was very well organised, by the way): 1. Political shifts can affect trust in expertise and the space universities have to contribute to public debate. 2. Economic pressure shapes what institutions can invest in and how secure academic careers feel. 3. Technological change, especially AI, is reshaping expectations around teaching, research and the skills academics need. 4. Societal change brings new demands for relevance, inclusion and flexibility. 5. Environmental challenges are prompting universities to rethink their responsibilities and long-term choices. What interests me most is how these developments connect, and how well universities can respond to change across all these areas. Expectations to contribute through teaching, research, public engagement and collaboration can expand academic workloads. Within that complexity, one question keeps resurfacing: what kinds of academic work are recognised when careers progress? One theme in today’s discussions that resonated with me was the recognition of teaching in academic careers. Teaching is central to a university’s purpose, yet its place in career progression remains an important question across higher education. The discussion also raised a broader challenge: staff development cannot simply mean adding new skills to already full workloads. It depends on whether institutions create the time, pathways and recognition that allow people to develop and contribute sustainably. The Research Science Institute (RSI) is one of the most prestigious and selective summer research programs in the world for high school students. Each summer, only 100 students are selected to take part at MIT; the acceptance rate is around 2%, the program is completely free, and close to one third of its participants come from outside the United States. And starting in 2027, this opportunity will also expand to Stanford University. For six weeks, selected students do far more than simply take a course at MIT. They work with researchers, develop an original scientific project, write a research paper, and present their results at the RSI Symposium. It is an experience designed for students who have already taken mathematics, physics, biology, computer science, or engineering far beyond what is normally studied in high school. In the new RUTA blog article, we explain what the Research Science Institute really is, how it began, who can apply, how the application process works for U.S. and international students, what kind of profiles are typically selected, what happens during the six weeks, and why RSI can become one of the strongest academic experiences in a STEM profile. We also discuss an important distinction that many families do not fully understand: not every summer program that carries the name of a prestigious university has the same academic value. Spending a few weeks studying at Harvard, Columbia, Brown, Cornell, Georgetown, or NYU is very different from earning a place in a highly selective program such as RSI, SSP, or PROMYS, where admission itself already represents a significant academic distinction. And the next edition will be especially interesting. In 2027, RSI will keep its 100 places at MIT and add another 50 at Stanford, marking the largest expansion in the program’s history. About Leiden University
Basic information and contact details for Leiden University
Founded in 1575, Leiden University is the first university in the Netherlands and a broad, internationally oriented research university. Across seven faculties in two cities, Leiden and The Hague, more than 33,000 students from 120 nationalities learn to tackle the challenges of today and tomorrow.

Are you curious, critical and involved in the world around you? At Leiden University you can make a valuable contribution to tackling the national and international challenges facing modern society. Together with academics and fellow students from all over the world, you will actively address these challenges. We keep an open mind, do not shy away from difficult discussions and allow one another the space to disagree. We expect the same active, open-minded and critical attitude from you.
Bastion of freedom. William of Orange founded the university in 1575, it is said in recognition of the city's courageous resistance against the Spanish siege. Our motto, Praesidium Libertatis (bastion of freedom), still guides us: we place great value on freedom of thought, inquiry and speech. Sixteen Nobel Prize winners have been connected to Leiden.
Teaching with personal attention. Our teaching is characterised by individual attention for students, contact with diverse cultures and innovative teaching methods. Our modest community size in the historical cities of Leiden and The Hague creates a personal and committed atmosphere. Together, we map out a learning path that suits you and your ambitions, and you are encouraged to conduct research with eminent and enthusiastic scholars. Teaching and research are closely interwoven.
Research that matters. Our research and teaching inspire one another, and this cross-pollination shapes our contribution to society. We train our students to become analytical thinkers and critical world citizens who can apply their knowledge to make the world a safe, healthy, sustainable, prosperous and just place.
Two cities, one university. Leiden is a real student city: a historic and lively centre with university buildings, student associations, cafés and housing within cycling distance. The Hague, the city of peace and justice, is the political heart of the Netherlands and home to embassies, multinationals and international courts. Teaching and research at Campus The Hague focus on international law, peace and security, global affairs, governance and urban issues. The cities themselves are the campus.

Programmes. Leiden offers 51 bachelor's programmes and 83 master's programmes, many of them taught in English, across Archaeology, Governance and Global Affairs, Humanities, Law, Medicine, Science, and Social and Behavioural Sciences. Explore our master's programmes, or read about admission and application. (https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/education/masters?utm_source=THE&utm_medium=portal&utm_campaign=Enhanced+Profile&utm_content=description_masters), (https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/education/admission-and-application?utm_source=THE&utm_medium=portal&utm_campaign=Enhanced+Profile&utm_content=description_admission).
Support and career. Every faculty has its own career services, open to students and to alumni for up to one year after graduation. Career counsellors help with internships, job applications and planning your next step, in the Netherlands or abroad. Leiden's lecturers and professors bring an extensive network of international organisations, companies and research institutes.
More than our rank. Leiden University often appears high in international rankings, but we encourage you to look beyond them and explore who we are: a university that values academic freedom, open debate and an engaged community. Find out why students choose Leiden (https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/education/masters/why-leiden-university?utm_source=THE&utm_medium=portal&utm_campaign=Enhanced+Profile&utm_content=description_why_leiden).
Leiden University welcomes anyone who wants to achieve their full potential. The knowledge and skills you develop here will benefit you for the rest of your life, whatever career path you choose.

Six universities in the Netherlands have ranked in the top 100 universities worldwide, according to the World University Rankings 2024, as compiled by Times Higher Education. Delft retains its spot as the best university overall in the Netherlands.

# 6 Dutch universities ranked among the top 100 in the world
## World University Rankings 2024 studies institutions in 166 different countries
The Times Higher Education ranking scores universities on 18 carefully selected performance indicators, updated this year to reflect the outputs of the diverse range of universities located across the world.
These performance indicators are grouped into five areas: Teaching (the learning environment); Research environment (volume, income and reputation); Research quality (citation impact, research strength, research excellence and research influence); International outlook (staff, students and research); and Industry (income and patents).
Naturally, not all of these areas have an equal weight in the ranking, with Teaching weighted at 29,5 percent, Research Environment at 29 percent, Research Quality at 30 percent, International Outlook at 7,5 percent and Industry at 4 percent. The ranking looks at data, combined with the results of the Academic Reputation Survey 2023, where more than 500.000 votes were analysed to draw conclusions about universities in 166 different countries.

# 6 Dutch universities ranked among the top 100 in the world
## Six Dutch universities make the top 100 in the World University Rankings 2024
The six Dutch universities featured in the top 100 are: Delft University of Technology, the University of Amsterdam, Wageningen University and Research, Leiden University, University of Groningen and the Erasmus University Rotterdam. The top Dutch university, Delft, came in 48th place, ahead of its 2023 spot in 70th position.
TU Delft is a research university home to around 16.000 students, many of whom are international students, which produces world-leading research and has strong strategic partnerships with industry, including many Dutch companies.The university offers all of its master’s degree programmes in English. However those looking to undertake an undergraduate degree at the school will first need to do a few Dutch courses, since most of them are taught in Dutch.
The Dutch university in the lowest spot, according to the ranking, is Tilburg University. Interestingly, the Dutch university with the lowest number of international students was named as Radboud University (ranked 140th), where of the 23.004 students, only 12 percent are internationals.

# 6 Dutch universities ranked among the top 100 in the world
## Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2024
The top Dutch universities for 2024 according to the World University Rankings are:
*   48. Delft University of Technology  
*   61. University of Amsterdam  
*   64. Wageningen University and Research  
*   77. Leiden University  
*   79. University of Groningen  
*   99. Erasmus University Rotterdam
As for the global top 10, the winners are:
*   1. University of Oxford  
*   2. Stanford University  
*   3. Massachusetts University of Technology  
*   4. Harvard University  
*   5. University of Cambridge  
*   6. Princeton University  
*   7. California Institute of Technology  
*   8. Imperial College London  
*   9. University of California, Berkeley  
*   10. Yale University
For the full list of universities, or more information on how the list was compiled, see the Times Higher Education website.

TheQS World University Rankingcompares 1.000 top universities on the following ten indicators:
*   Academic reputation, measured using a global survey of academics (30%);  
*   Citations per faculty score, based on Elsevier’s Scopus database (20%);  
*   Employer reputation, measured using a global survey of employers (15%);  
*   Employment outcomes, based on alumni impact metrics and graduate employment index (5%);  
*   Student-to-faculty ratio (10%)  
*   International student ratio (5%)  
*   International faculty ratio (5%)  
*   International research network (5%)  
*   Sustainability (5%).
The QS ranking, which casts its net more broadly than the ARWU, also ranks universities by 55 different subjects. The order in which the QS and ARWU rankings place universities differs because they are based on a different set of indicators. The ARWU ranking is based on factual scientific output, while the QS ranking also uses indicators on reputation, studentoutcomes and sustainability.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **Times Higher Education Ranking**
The Times Higher Education (THE) has publishedTHE World University Rankings since 2004. Like the QS World University Rankings, it covers a broad spectrum of university activities: teaching (30%), research environment (29%), research quality (30%), industry (4%) and international outlook (7.5%). One third of the scores is based on the Academic Reputation Survey. The THE methodology is much-criticised. Because of changes in the methodology, the makers strongly advise against direct comparisons with previous years’ World University Rankings.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **The Leiden Ranking**
TheLeiden Ranking is compiled by the Centre for Science and Technology Studies (CWTS) at Leiden University. It goes even further than the ARWU in focusing specifically on research, as it is based solely on bibliometric data (publications and citations) from the Web of Science scientific citation indexing service. That also explains why it focuses mainly on the natural and medical sciences, which traditionally publish in international science journals. The Leiden Ranking is an interactive index of over 1300 research universities world-wide.Users can set their own parameters:
*   Time period: the first available time period is 2006-2009, with each successive period being one year later in time;  
*   Field: one of the five fields of science or all sciences;  
*   Region/country;  
*   Minimum publication output;  
*   Type of indicator: 'impact', 'collaboration' (based on co-authored publications) and since 2019 also 'open access' and 'gender';  
*   Citation-impact indicators (including top 1%, top 5%, top 10% and top 50%)  
*   Collaboration indicators (total no. of publications co-authored with other organisations, no. of publications co-authored with other countries, no. of publications co-authored with industry, and no. of co-authored publications based on distance, either <100 km or >5000 km).
Since 2024 the Centre for Science and Technology Studies also offers the CWTS Leiden Ranking Open Edition. In this ranking, bibliometric data is from the OpenAlex database. A university’s standing on the Leiden ranking may vary considerably depending on the indicator used, as shown in the table below.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **U-Multirank**
A new type of university performance table was launched in 2014 with the financial support of the European Commission. It was developed by a consortium led by the Centre for Higher Education (CHE) in Germany and the Center for Higher Education Policy Studies (CHEPS) and CWTS in the Netherlands. U-Multirank is not so much a ranking as a tool for comparing university performance on five dimensions and thirty aspects, based on information about more than 1300 institutions of higher education. Performance is rated on a scale ranging from very good (A ) to weak (E).The dimensions are:
*   teaching and learning;  
*   regional engagement;  
*   knowledge transfer;  
*   international orientation;  
*   research.
The U-Multirank has a number of ‘readymade’ rankings on its website. One of these focuses on research and research linkages. The results of the Dutch universities on the 'readymade' ranking research and research collaboration is presented in aseparate file for the years 2017-2022. It shows that almost all Dutch universities received the highest score (A: very good) on the indicators _citation rate_ and _research publications_ (size-normalized). All Dutch universities scored the highest score on _top cited publications_(the proportion of a university’s publications that, compared with other publications in the same field and in the same year, belong to the top 10% most frequently cited). All universities scored an A (very good) on the indicator _co-publications with industrial partners_, except for Tilburg University. The indicators _international joint publications_ and _regional joint publications_ showed a more diverse pattern. On the latter, we foundmuch more C (average) and D (below average) scores. Since January 2025 the U-multirank has been incorporated in theEuropean Higher Education Sector Scoreboard of the European Commission. Currently, the scoreboard includes data upto the year 2022.

**Global rankings of universities have been published regularly for the past two decades.Shanghai Jiao Tong University's Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) in China was the first in June 2003 and many others followed. 'Rankings of universities should be used with caution,' says Leiden-Delft-Erasmus Dean Prof. dr. Wim van den Doel. 'A lot is being measured, but a lot is also left unseen.' Nevertheless, we want to know: how do the Zuid-Holland universities, Leiden University, TU Delft and Erasmus University Rotterdam, position themselves in these lists?**
Leiden University, TU Delft and Erasmus University Rotterdam can be found in different places in the various university rankings. All three can rightfully claim to be a global top 100 university. And because there are more than 20,000 universities worldwide, they are also among the top 1% in the world. In certain fields, in particular, the Leiden-Delft-Erasmus universities are among the absolute best in the world.
'Rankings of universities should be used with caution,' says LDE dean Prof. dr. Wim van den Doel. 'A lot is measured, but a lot is also left unseen. Sometimes the social sciences and humanities are not included, sometimes they are, and while these are quantifiable variables, the quality of education, for example, is difficult to quantify. Nevertheless, the rankings also say something. As far as the Leiden-Delft-Erasmus universities are concerned, in any case, they demonstrate high quality in different rankings'.
Van den Doel explicitly refers to the rankings per subject as drawn up by _Times Higher Education_ and _QS Quacquarelli Symonds_. The opinions of academics and employers are combined with bibliometric data. 'You can see how good the universities in Zuid Holland are, especially in the rankings per discipline. Almost always in the top 100, often in the top 50 and sometimes even in the top 10 in the world. Certainly, something to be proud of'.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **QS World University Ranking**
TheQS World University Rankingcompares 1.000 top universities on the following ten indicators:
*   Academic reputation, measured using a global survey of academics (30%);  
*   Citations per faculty score, based on Elsevier’s Scopus database (20%);  
*   Employer reputation, measured using a global survey of employers (15%);  
*   Employment outcomes, based on alumni impact metrics and graduate employment index (5%);  
*   Student-to-faculty ratio (10%)  
*   International student ratio (5%)  
*   International faculty ratio (5%)  
*   International research network (5%)  
*   Sustainability (5%).
The QS ranking, which casts its net more broadly than the ARWU, also ranks universities by 55 different subjects. The order in which the QS and ARWU rankings place universities differs because they are based on a different set of indicators. The ARWU ranking is based on factual scientific output, while the QS ranking also uses indicators on reputation, studentoutcomes and sustainability.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **Times Higher Education Ranking**
The Times Higher Education (THE) has publishedTHE World University Rankings since 2004. Like the QS World University Rankings, it covers a broad spectrum of university activities: teaching (30%), research environment (29%), research quality (30%), industry (4%) and international outlook (7.5%). One third of the scores is based on the Academic Reputation Survey. The THE methodology is much-criticised. Because of changes in the methodology, the makers strongly advise against direct comparisons with previous years’ World University Rankings.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **The Leiden Ranking**
TheLeiden Ranking is compiled by the Centre for Science and Technology Studies (CWTS) at Leiden University. It goes even further than the ARWU in focusing specifically on research, as it is based solely on bibliometric data (publications and citations) from the Web of Science scientific citation indexing service. That also explains why it focuses mainly on the natural and medical sciences, which traditionally publish in international science journals. The Leiden Ranking is an interactive index of over 1300 research universities world-wide.Users can set their own parameters:
*   Time period: the first available time period is 2006-2009, with each successive period being one year later in time;  
*   Field: one of the five fields of science or all sciences;  
*   Region/country;  
*   Minimum publication output;  
*   Type of indicator: 'impact', 'collaboration' (based on co-authored publications) and since 2019 also 'open access' and 'gender';  
*   Citation-impact indicators (including top 1%, top 5%, top 10% and top 50%)  
*   Collaboration indicators (total no. of publications co-authored with other organisations, no. of publications co-authored with other countries, no. of publications co-authored with industry, and no. of co-authored publications based on distance, either <100 km or >5000 km).
Since 2024 the Centre for Science and Technology Studies also offers the CWTS Leiden Ranking Open Edition. In this ranking, bibliometric data is from the OpenAlex database. A university’s standing on the Leiden ranking may vary considerably depending on the indicator used, as shown in the table below.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **U-Multirank**
A new type of university performance table was launched in 2014 with the financial support of the European Commission. It was developed by a consortium led by the Centre for Higher Education (CHE) in Germany and the Center for Higher Education Policy Studies (CHEPS) and CWTS in the Netherlands. U-Multirank is not so much a ranking as a tool for comparing university performance on five dimensions and thirty aspects, based on information about more than 1300 institutions of higher education. Performance is rated on a scale ranging from very good (A ) to weak (E).The dimensions are:
*   teaching and learning;  
*   regional engagement;  
*   knowledge transfer;  
*   international orientation;  
*   research.
The U-Multirank has a number of ‘readymade’ rankings on its website. One of these focuses on research and research linkages. The results of the Dutch universities on the 'readymade' ranking research and research collaboration is presented in aseparate file for the years 2017-2022. It shows that almost all Dutch universities received the highest score (A: very good) on the indicators _citation rate_ and _research publications_ (size-normalized). All Dutch universities scored the highest score on _top cited publications_(the proportion of a university’s publications that, compared with other publications in the same field and in the same year, belong to the top 10% most frequently cited). All universities scored an A (very good) on the indicator _co-publications with industrial partners_, except for Tilburg University. The indicators _international joint publications_ and _regional joint publications_ showed a more diverse pattern. On the latter, we foundmuch more C (average) and D (below average) scores. Since January 2025 the U-multirank has been incorporated in theEuropean Higher Education Sector Scoreboard of the European Commission. Currently, the scoreboard includes data upto the year 2022.

Title: Rankings: the Leiden-Delft-Erasmus Universities are among the best of the world
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
**Global rankings of universities have been published regularly for the past two decades.Shanghai Jiao Tong University's Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) in China was the first in June 2003 and many others followed. 'Rankings of universities should be used with caution,' says Leiden-Delft-Erasmus Dean Prof. dr. Wim van den Doel. 'A lot is being measured, but a lot is also left unseen.' Nevertheless, we want to know: how do the Zuid-Holland universities, Leiden University, TU Delft and Erasmus University Rotterdam, position themselves in these lists?**
Leiden University, TU Delft and Erasmus University Rotterdam can be found in different places in the various university rankings. All three can rightfully claim to be a global top 100 university. And because there are more than 20,000 universities worldwide, they are also among the top 1% in the world. In certain fields, in particular, the Leiden-Delft-Erasmus universities are among the absolute best in the world.
'Rankings of universities should be used with caution,' says LDE dean Prof. dr. Wim van den Doel. 'A lot is measured, but a lot is also left unseen. Sometimes the social sciences and humanities are not included, sometimes they are, and while these are quantifiable variables, the quality of education, for example, is difficult to quantify. Nevertheless, the rankings also say something. As far as the Leiden-Delft-Erasmus universities are concerned, in any case, they demonstrate high quality in different rankings'.
Van den Doel explicitly refers to the rankings per subject as drawn up by _Times Higher Education_ and _QS Quacquarelli Symonds_. The opinions of academics and employers are combined with bibliometric data. 'You can see how good the universities in Zuid Holland are, especially in the rankings per discipline. Almost always in the top 100, often in the top 50 and sometimes even in the top 10 in the world. Certainly, something to be proud of'.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **QS World University Ranking**
TheQS World University Rankingcompares 1.000 top universities on the following ten indicators:
*   Academic reputation, measured using a global survey of academics (30%);  
*   Citations per faculty score, based on Elsevier’s Scopus database (20%);  
*   Employer reputation, measured using a global survey of employers (15%);  
*   Employment outcomes, based on alumni impact metrics and graduate employment index (5%);  
*   Student-to-faculty ratio (10%)  
*   International student ratio (5%)  
*   International faculty ratio (5%)  
*   International research network (5%)  
*   Sustainability (5%).
The QS ranking, which casts its net more broadly than the ARWU, also ranks universities by 55 different subjects. The order in which the QS and ARWU rankings place universities differs because they are based on a different set of indicators. The ARWU ranking is based on factual scientific output, while the QS ranking also uses indicators on reputation, studentoutcomes and sustainability.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **Times Higher Education Ranking**
The Times Higher Education (THE) has publishedTHE World University Rankings since 2004. Like the QS World University Rankings, it covers a broad spectrum of university activities: teaching (30%), research environment (29%), research quality (30%), industry (4%) and international outlook (7.5%). One third of the scores is based on the Academic Reputation Survey. The THE methodology is much-criticised. Because of changes in the methodology, the makers strongly advise against direct comparisons with previous years’ World University Rankings.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **The Leiden Ranking**
TheLeiden Ranking is compiled by the Centre for Science and Technology Studies (CWTS) at Leiden University. It goes even further than the ARWU in focusing specifically on research, as it is based solely on bibliometric data (publications and citations) from the Web of Science scientific citation indexing service. That also explains why it focuses mainly on the natural and medical sciences, which traditionally publish in international science journals. The Leiden Ranking is an interactive index of over 1300 research universities world-wide.Users can set their own parameters:
*   Time period: the first available time period is 2006-2009, with each successive period being one year later in time;  
*   Field: one of the five fields of science or all sciences;  
*   Region/country;  
*   Minimum publication output;  
*   Type of indicator: 'impact', 'collaboration' (based on co-authored publications) and since 2019 also 'open access' and 'gender';  
*   Citation-impact indicators (including top 1%, top 5%, top 10% and top 50%)  
*   Collaboration indicators (total no. of publications co-authored with other organisations, no. of publications co-authored with other countries, no. of publications co-authored with industry, and no. of co-authored publications based on distance, either <100 km or >5000 km).
Since 2024 the Centre for Science and Technology Studies also offers the CWTS Leiden Ranking Open Edition. In this ranking, bibliometric data is from the OpenAlex database. A university’s standing on the Leiden ranking may vary considerably depending on the indicator used, as shown in the table below.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **U-Multirank**
A new type of university performance table was launched in 2014 with the financial support of the European Commission. It was developed by a consortium led by the Centre for Higher Education (CHE) in Germany and the Center for Higher Education Policy Studies (CHEPS) and CWTS in the Netherlands. U-Multirank is not so much a ranking as a tool for comparing university performance on five dimensions and thirty aspects, based on information about more than 1300 institutions of higher education. Performance is rated on a scale ranging from very good (A ) to weak (E).The dimensions are:
*   teaching and learning;  
*   regional engagement;  
*   knowledge transfer;  
*   international orientation;  
*   research.
The U-Multirank has a number of ‘readymade’ rankings on its website. One of these focuses on research and research linkages. The results of the Dutch universities on the 'readymade' ranking research and research collaboration is presented in aseparate file for the years 2017-2022. It shows that almost all Dutch universities received the highest score (A: very good) on the indicators _citation rate_ and _research publications_ (size-normalized). All Dutch universities scored the highest score on _top cited publications_(the proportion of a university’s publications that, compared with other publications in the same field and in the same year, belong to the top 10% most frequently cited). All universities scored an A (very good) on the indicator _co-publications with industrial partners_, except for Tilburg University. The indicators _international joint publications_ and _regional joint publications_ showed a more diverse pattern. On the latter, we foundmuch more C (average) and D (below average) scores. Since January 2025 the U-multirank has been incorporated in theEuropean Higher Education Sector Scoreboard of the European Commission. Currently, the scoreboard includes data upto the year 2022.

PP(top 10%): The proportion of a university’s publications that, compared with other publications in the same field and in the same year, belong to the top 10% most frequently cited. Leiden ranking PP(collab): The proportion of a university’s publications that have been co-authored with one or more other organisations.Leiden ranking PP(industry): The proportion of a university’s publications that have been co-authored with industry.
The table above shows a varied picture of the position of Dutch universities, which can be explained by the diversity of methodologies: in some rankings only a single Dutch university is in the top 100, while in others almost half of them are. The table also shows that most universities do appear in the top 100 of one or more rankings. For example, Utrecht University has been the highest-scoring Dutch university in the Shanghai Ranking for years. In the QS Ranking, the Netherlands had as many as six universities in the top 100 in 2014/2015. In the years that followed, this number fluctuated between two and three universities, with the University of Amsterdam and TU Delft in the top 100 in 2027. In the THE Ranking, slightly fewer than half of the Dutch universities are in the top 100. Utrecht University has no longer participated in the THE Ranking since 2024. In the Leiden Ranking PP(industry), Eindhoven University of Technology takes a top position at rank 25.

# Rankings
## **Results of various rankings**
Dutch universities can also be found in the top 100 of the rankings by discipline or field of study. In the Shanghai Ranking by subject (Global Ranking of Academic Subjects, 2026), at least one Dutch university is represented in 48 of the 57 disciplines (the exceptions are ‘Telecommunication Engineering’, ‘Materials Science & Engineering’, ‘Nanoscience & Nanotechnology’, ‘Textile Science & Engineering’, ‘Mining & Mineral Engineering’, ‘Biomedical Engineering’, ‘Artificial Intelligence’, ‘Hospitality & Tourism Management’ and ‘Mathematics’). In ‘Psychology’, as many as nine Dutch universities are represented in the top 100, and in ‘Medical Technology’ and ‘Law’ eight. In the THE subject ranking for 2026, at least two Dutch universities are in the top 100 in all eleven broad fields of science. In the QS Subject Ranking 2026, at least one Dutch university is present in the top 50 in as many as 45 of the 55 disciplines.
In addition to their position in the ranking, universities can also be compared in other ways, by looking at size (based on total budget) and the teaching function (based on the number of enrolled students). The budget per student differs enormously between universities (the source is the ETER database, which contains data on European higher education institutions).

# Rankings
## **International comparison**
The table below shows the number of universities in the top 100 of various university rankings. Universities from the United States are by far the most represented, with 122 top-100 entries across the various rankings. They are followed by China and the United Kingdom with 62 and 50 top-100 entries respectively. The Netherlands has 14 top-100 entries in these university rankings. At first glance, this seems much less often than universities from the United States or China. However, these countries have many more universities than the Netherlands. The United States has 15 times as many universities, and the number of universities in China is even 28 times higher than in the Netherlands. The Netherlands has 13 universities. The fact that there are 14 top-100 entries is because universities can appear in multiple rankings. According to the CWTS Leiden Ranking Traditional Edition 2026, the country with the most universities in the world is China, with 366 universities.

At first glance, this seems much less often than universities from the United States or China. However, these countries have many more universities than the Netherlands. The United States has 15 times as many universities, and the number of universities in China is even 28 times higher than in the Netherlands. The Netherlands has 13 universities. The fact that there are 14 top-100 entries is because universities can appear in multiple rankings. # Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **QS World University Ranking**
TheQS World University Rankingcompares 1.000 top universities on the following ten indicators:
*   Academic reputation, measured using a global survey of academics (30%);  
*   Citations per faculty score, based on Elsevier’s Scopus database (20%);  
*   Employer reputation, measured using a global survey of employers (15%);  
*   Employment outcomes, based on alumni impact metrics and graduate employment index (5%);  
*   Student-to-faculty ratio (10%)  
*   International student ratio (5%)  
*   International faculty ratio (5%)  
*   International research network (5%)  
*   Sustainability (5%).
The QS ranking, which casts its net more broadly than the ARWU, also ranks universities by 55 different subjects. The order in which the QS and ARWU rankings place universities differs because they are based on a different set of indicators. The ARWU ranking is based on factual scientific output, while the QS ranking also uses indicators on reputation, studentoutcomes and sustainability.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **Times Higher Education Ranking**
The Times Higher Education (THE) has publishedTHE World University Rankings since 2004. Like the QS World University Rankings, it covers a broad spectrum of university activities: teaching (30%), research environment (29%), research quality (30%), industry (4%) and international outlook (7.5%). One third of the scores is based on the Academic Reputation Survey. The THE methodology is much-criticised. Because of changes in the methodology, the makers strongly advise against direct comparisons with previous years’ World University Rankings.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **The Leiden Ranking**
TheLeiden Ranking is compiled by the Centre for Science and Technology Studies (CWTS) at Leiden University. It goes even further than the ARWU in focusing specifically on research, as it is based solely on bibliometric data (publications and citations) from the Web of Science scientific citation indexing service. That also explains why it focuses mainly on the natural and medical sciences, which traditionally publish in international science journals. The Leiden Ranking is an interactive index of over 1300 research universities world-wide.Users can set their own parameters:
*   Time period: the first available time period is 2006-2009, with each successive period being one year later in time;  
*   Field: one of the five fields of science or all sciences;  
*   Region/country;  
*   Minimum publication output;  
*   Type of indicator: 'impact', 'collaboration' (based on co-authored publications) and since 2019 also 'open access' and 'gender';  
*   Citation-impact indicators (including top 1%, top 5%, top 10% and top 50%)  
*   Collaboration indicators (total no. of publications co-authored with other organisations, no. of publications co-authored with other countries, no. of publications co-authored with industry, and no. of co-authored publications based on distance, either <100 km or >5000 km).
Since 2024 the Centre for Science and Technology Studies also offers the CWTS Leiden Ranking Open Edition. In this ranking, bibliometric data is from the OpenAlex database. A university’s standing on the Leiden ranking may vary considerably depending on the indicator used, as shown in the table below.

# Rankings
## **2. University rankings**
### **U-Multirank**
A new type of university performance table was launched in 2014 with the financial support of the European Commission. It was developed by a consortium led by the Centre for Higher Education (CHE) in Germany and the Center for Higher Education Policy Studies (CHEPS) and CWTS in the Netherlands. U-Multirank is not so much a ranking as a tool for comparing university performance on five dimensions and thirty aspects, based on information about more than 1300 institutions of higher education. Performance is rated on a scale ranging from very good (A ) to weak (E).The dimensions are:
*   teaching and learning;  
*   regional engagement;  
*   knowledge transfer;  
*   international orientation;  
*   research.
The U-Multirank has a number of ‘readymade’ rankings on its website. One of these focuses on research and research linkages. The results of the Dutch universities on the 'readymade' ranking research and research collaboration is presented in aseparate file for the years 2017-2022. It shows that almost all Dutch universities received the highest score (A: very good) on the indicators _citation rate_ and _research publications_ (size-normalized). All Dutch universities scored the highest score on _top cited publications_(the proportion of a university’s publications that, compared with other publications in the same field and in the same year, belong to the top 10% most frequently cited). All universities scored an A (very good) on the indicator _co-publications with industrial partners_, except for Tilburg University. The indicators _international joint publications_ and _regional joint publications_ showed a more diverse pattern. On the latter, we foundmuch more C (average) and D (below average) scores. Since January 2025 the U-multirank has been incorporated in theEuropean Higher Education Sector Scoreboard of the European Commission. Currently, the scoreboard includes data upto the year 2022.

## Answer

**Yes, several Dutch universities had Research Quality scores of 60 or above in all three years (2021, 2022, and 2023).** The times higher education rankings typically report both Overall and Pillar scores (including Teaching, Research Environment, Research Quality, Industry, and International Outlook).

Here are the Dutch universities that consistently achieved **Research Quality scores ≥60** across all three editions (2021, 2022, and 2023):
